Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

vignette: Maryam, a 77-year-old Middle Eastern woman who is single and works as a tutor, has been profoundly affected by her experiences during the war in her home country. The traumatic event she witnessed—a bombing that destroyed her neighborhood and left many of her neighbors dead or injured—has etched itself deeply into her psyche. To this day, remembering those moments brings back the same paralyzing terror she felt at the time. When triggered, which can happen without warning by seemingly mundane things like the sound of a door slamming or an unexpected loud noise, Maryam feels as if she is reliving that horrific experience. Maryam had come to believe that she was emotionally numb and dead inside, and thinking about the event would be too much for her to handle. This belief led her to avoid any media coverage related to war, including TV programs, films, or even reading about similar events in newspapers. Her sense of weakness only deepened this avoidance behavior; staying near exits at all times became a way to feel somewhat safe and in control. The more Maryam avoided thinking about the event by staying close to exits and avoiding media coverage, the more her memories seemed to haunt her unexpectedly. The terror that accompanied these intrusive thoughts reinforced her negative beliefs about herself and her ability to cope with trauma. As she dwelled on how she used to be before the event—a vibrant and social person who enjoyed her work and community activities—she felt increasingly isolated. Maryam’s avoidance behaviors had concrete consequences in her daily life. Her job as a tutor required her to interact with students, but her preoccupation with staying near exits made it difficult for her to fully engage in their learning process. She often found herself distracted or even absent from class if she perceived the environment as too unsafe. This led to strained relationships with some of her students and colleagues who noticed a marked change in her demeanor. What frightened Maryam most was the loss of control over her life and the fear that she would never be able to move past these memories. The thought of reliving those moments every day became unbearable, and she had begun to realize that her current strategies were not sustainable. Despite feeling emotionally numb and weak, she recognized that seeking help might offer a path towards reclaiming some sense of normalcy and control over her life. Maryam’s journey to seek therapy was prompted by an incident where she almost left work early in the middle of a lesson because she thought she heard distant explosions—something that still triggered vivid flashbacks. This realization, coupled with the guilt she felt for not being able to fully support her students, pushed her towards seeking professional help. She is most hoping that therapy can provide tools and strategies to manage her intrusive memories and regain some semblance of emotional connection to the world around her.
